section.title: The Plague of Locusts
section.sectionRationale: The eighth plague forms its own scene, opening with God's explicit purpose that Israel will one day tell their children of this history, moving through Pharaoh's officials pressuring him, the negotiation over who may go, the devastating locusts, and another swift, broken confession.
section.thesis: God tells Moses plainly that these signs are meant to become family memory, told to children and grandchildren for generations, even as Pharaoh's officials themselves plead with him to relent and Pharaoh still tries to bargain over who gets to leave.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: God's purpose that Israel will retell this to their children; Pharaoh's officials pressuring him and the negotiation over who may go; the locusts devouring everything the hail had spared; Pharaoh's swift confession and equally swift hardening.

units.label: That you may tell your children

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his officials, that I may perform these miraculous signs of Mine among them,
and that you may tell your children and grandchildren how severely I dealt with the Egyptians when I performed miraculous signs among them, so that all of you may know that I am the LORD.”

So Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and told him, “This is what the LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says: ‘How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me? Let My people go, so that they may worship Me.
But if you refuse to let My people go, I will bring {{arbeh|locusts}} into your territory tomorrow.
They will cover the face of the land so that no one can see it. They will devour whatever is left after the hail and eat every tree that grows in your fields.

They will fill your houses and the houses of all your officials and every Egyptian, something neither your fathers nor your grandfathers have seen since the day they came into this land.’” Then Moses turned and left Pharaoh's presence.

units.label: How long will this man be a snare?

verses.text: Pharaoh's officials asked him, “How long will this man be a snare to us? Let the people go, so that they may worship the LORD their God. Do you not yet realize that Egypt is in ruins?”
So Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh. “Go, worship the LORD your God,” he said. “But who exactly will be going?”
“We will go with our young and old,” Moses replied. “We will go with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds, for we must hold a feast to the LORD.”
Then Pharaoh told them, “May the LORD be with you if I ever let you go with your little ones. Clearly you are bent on evil.
No, only the men may go and worship the LORD, since that is what you have been requesting.” And Moses and Aaron were driven from Pharaoh's presence.

units.label: Nothing green was left
units.note: the locusts devour what the hail spared

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses, “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, so that the locusts may swarm over it and devour every plant in the land, everything that the hail has left behind.”
So Moses stretched out his staff over the land of Egypt, and throughout that day and night the LORD sent an east wind across the land. By morning the east wind had brought the locusts.
The locusts swarmed across the land and settled over the entire territory of Egypt. Never before had there been so many locusts, and never again will there be.

They covered the face of all the land until it was black, and they consumed all the plants on the ground and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had left behind. Nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh quickly summoned Moses and Aaron and said, “I have sinned against the LORD your God and against you.
Now please forgive my sin once more and appeal to the LORD your God, that He may remove this death from me.”
So Moses left Pharaoh's presence and appealed to the LORD.
And the LORD changed the wind to a very strong west wind that carried off the locusts and blew them into the Red Sea. Not a single locust remained anywhere in Egypt.
But the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, and he would not let the Israelites go.

arbeh.gloss: Locusts, one of the most feared agricultural disasters in the ancient world, capable of stripping a land bare within hours. The same word describes the devastating locust plague in Joel 1 to 2, later read as an image of the coming day of the LORD.

basic.context: This is the eighth plague. God tells Moses this history is meant to be remembered and told to children for generations. Pharaoh's own officials plead with him to relent since Egypt lies in ruins, and Pharaoh tries again to negotiate limited terms, only letting the men go. When Moses refuses, the locusts come, devouring every green thing the hail had spared. Pharaoh confesses again and asks forgiveness, but the moment relief comes, his heart hardens once more.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history, and it explicitly tells us why: so that Israel would tell their children and grandchildren for generations what God had done. It also shows Pharaoh's negotiating tactics escalating, willing to let some go but not all, a partial obedience Scripture treats as no true obedience.
basic.originalLanguages: The plague brings arbeh, locusts, the same devastating creature described in Joel's prophecy as an image of the coming day of the LORD, capable of stripping an entire land bare within hours, exactly what happens here to everything the hail had spared.
basic.typology: The locust plague, devouring everything green, anticipates Joel's prophetic use of locusts as a picture of divine judgment on a covenant people who have strayed, later transformed in Joel 2:28-32 into a promise of restoration and outpoured Spirit, fulfilled at Pentecost, Acts 2:16-21.
basic.christ: God's stated purpose, that this history be told to children and grandchildren, anticipates the pattern of covenant remembrance culminating in the Lord's Supper, do this in remembrance of Me, Luke 22:19, where God's people continue to retell and reenact His decisive act of redemption across every generation.
basic.god: God is intentional not only about acting in history but about that history being remembered and retold, weaving remembrance into the very purpose of the plagues. He is also patient with negotiation up to a point, yet He does not accept Pharaoh's partial, self-serving compromises over who may worship Him.
basic.crossReferences: Joel 1:4 and 2:25 describe a locust plague as devastating judgment later reversed by God's mercy. Psalm 78:46 and Psalm 105:34-35 recall this plague as one of God's mighty acts. Acts 2:16-21 shows Joel's later locust-framed prophecy fulfilled in the outpouring of the Spirit.
basic.oneStory: This is another devastating strike in Egypt's judgment, deliberately remembered and retold across generations, and it exposes Pharaoh's continued pattern of partial, self-interested concessions. It anticipates how God's people are called to remember and retell His saving acts, a pattern completed in the ongoing remembrance of Christ's greater deliverance.

context.literary:
The eighth plague opens in an unusual way. Before Moses says a word to Pharaoh, God speaks to Moses about Israel, verses 1 and 2. The first seven plagues were each introduced by a message for the king; this one is introduced by a message for the storytellers. The plagues are now being told with one eye on the future audience, the children and grandchildren who will hear them.

Two questions beginning "How long" frame the confrontation. Moses asks Pharaoh, "How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me?" verse 3, and the royal officials ask Pharaoh, "How long will this man be a snare to us?" verse 7. The king is squeezed from both sides. For the first time his own court breaks ranks before the plague falls, and Moses, having delivered the warning, simply "turned and left," verse 6, without waiting for an answer.

The negotiation of verses 8 to 11 is a small drama of its own. Pharaoh's question is literally "who and who are going?" Moses answers with a sweeping list in pairs, "young and old," "sons and daughters," "flocks and herds," verse 9, a way of saying everyone and everything. Pharaoh's reply narrows it to "only the men," verse 11, and the scene ends with Moses and Aaron "driven" from his presence. The verb is the same one God used when He promised that Pharaoh would one day "drive them out of his land," Exodus 6:1. The king is already doing, in miniature, what he will be forced to do in full.

The plague itself is framed by two winds. An east wind blows all day and night and brings the locusts, verse 13; a strong west wind carries them into the sea until "not a single locust remained," verse 19. Between the winds the land turns black and "nothing green was left," verse 15. The superlative of verse 14, "Never before had there been so many locusts, and never again will there be," anticipates the great cry of Exodus 11:6, and the chapter closes as the hail did: a quick confession, a removal of the plague, and a heart hardened again.
context.historical:
Locust swarms were among the most feared disasters of the ancient world. A swarm can arrive on the wind in numbers that darken the sky and cover the ground, and it strips crops, leaves and even bark before moving on. Joel's description of a land that is "like the Garden of Eden" before the swarm and "like a desert wasteland" behind it, Joel 2:3, captures what farmers across the region knew by experience. In Egypt the swarm came as the sequel to the hail. The wheat and spelt that had survived because they ripened later, Exodus 9:32, were exactly what the locusts now consumed, verse 15.

The officials' words in verse 7 reflect the scale of loss. "Egypt is in ruins" is literally "Egypt has perished." Egyptian kingship claimed to hold the land in order and plenty; a king under whom the fields had been beaten by hail and eaten by locusts was a king whose claim was visibly failing. Pharaoh's advisers were not converts. They were men counting the cost of their master's pride.

The dispute about who would go reflects real customs. Moses calls the journey a feast, chag, verse 9, the word for a pilgrimage festival. Israel's later festivals were family occasions, kept by "you, your sons and daughters, your menservants and maidservants," Deuteronomy 16:11 and 16:14. Moses is not inventing an excuse to take the children; he is describing what worship of the LORD had always involved. Pharaoh, for his part, understood leverage. Men who left wives, children and herds behind would have to come back. His offer of "only the men" was a way of keeping hostages.

The east wind makes geographical sense, since the deserts of Sinai and Arabia lie east of Egypt. The west wind that removes them is literally a "sea wind," because for a Hebrew speaker in Canaan the sea lay to the west. The locusts end in the yam suf, the same water that will soon swallow Pharaoh's army, Exodus 15:4.
context.canonical:
The command to tell children and grandchildren, verse 2, becomes one of the great threads of the Torah. It returns at the Passover, "When your children ask you, 'What does this service mean to you?'" Exodus 12:26, at the consecration of the firstborn, Exodus 13:14, and throughout Deuteronomy: "Teach them to your children and grandchildren," Deuteronomy 4:9, and, when a son asks what the commandments mean, "you are to tell him, 'We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt,'" Deuteronomy 6:20-21. Joshua sets up stones at the Jordan for the same purpose, Joshua 4:6-7, and Psalm 78:4-6 commits a whole generation to telling "the wonders He has performed" to "children yet to be born."

The locusts themselves become part of the covenant's warnings. Moses tells Israel that if they forsake the LORD, "the locusts will consume" their seed, Deuteronomy 28:38, and "the diseases you dreaded in Egypt" will cling to them, Deuteronomy 28:60. The plagues of Egypt could fall on Israel. Solomon prays about exactly that, 1 Kings 8:37, and God answers that if His people "humble themselves and pray," He will heal their land, 2 Chronicles 7:13-14. Amos sees a swarm prepared against Israel and intercedes as Moses did, and the LORD relents, Amos 7:1-3.

Joel builds his whole prophecy on this chapter. He opens with the same charge, "Tell it to your children," Joel 1:3, describes an invasion "such as never was of old, nor will ever be," Joel 2:2, echoing verse 14, and calls Israel to do what Pharaoh refused: "return to Me with all your heart," Joel 2:12. Then God promises to "repay you for the years eaten by locusts," Joel 2:25, and to pour out His Spirit on "your sons and daughters," Joel 2:28. Peter declares that promise fulfilled at Pentecost, Acts 2:16-21.

Revelation completes the thread with locusts rising from the Abyss, Revelation 9:3-11, a demonic swarm that torments those without God's seal. Even then, "the rest of mankind who were not killed by these plagues still did not repent," Revelation 9:20.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted every Israelite household to understand that it was part of this story. God says the signs were performed "that you may tell your children and grandchildren," and then adds, "so that all of you may know that I am the LORD," verse 2. The plagues were not only meant to teach Egypt. They were meant to form Israel's own knowledge of God, generation after generation. Faith in Israel was designed to be handed down by testimony, told in the ears of children.

He also meant Israel to see what pride looks like. God's charge against Pharaoh is not ignorance but refusal to "humble yourself," verse 3. The verb comes from the same root used for Egypt's oppression of Israel in Exodus 1:11-12. The king who humbled others would not be humbled himself. Later Moses tells Israel that God led them through the wilderness "so that He might humble you," Deuteronomy 8:2. Israel was to learn willingly the lesson Pharaoh would only learn by force.

And he meant Israel to understand that the LORD claims His whole people. Pharaoh was willing to let some worship. Moses insisted on young and old, sons and daughters, and animals for sacrifice. The worship of the LORD is not something one part of a household does on behalf of the rest while the others remain under another master. For a people about to be formed into a nation at Sinai, that insistence shaped what it meant to belong to God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes a unique judgment on a unique king. It does not teach that every swarm, drought or crop failure is a direct sign of God's anger against a particular people. Under the Sinai covenant God did tie such disasters to Israel's faithfulness in the land, Deuteronomy 28:38, but that covenant arrangement belonged to Israel's national life, and Jesus warned against reading disasters as a scorecard of guilt, Luke 13:4-5.

What does carry forward is explicit. Verse 2 is not only a description; it is a charge that the rest of Scripture repeats. Believing parents are still meant to tell their children what God has done, Ephesians 6:4 speaks of raising children "in the discipline and instruction of the Lord," and the church still retells its founding deliverance every time it takes the Lord's Supper. The refusal of partial terms carries forward as well. God's people cannot accept arrangements in which worship is permitted only on conditions set by a power that wants to keep hold of part of them.

debates.question: Was Pharaoh's offer to let only the men go a reasonable compromise or continued defiance?

views.label: A calculated way of keeping hostages
views.case: Moses had asked for everyone, verse 9, and Pharaoh's reply, "May the LORD be with you if I ever let you go with your little ones," verse 10, is sarcasm. With wives, children and herds left in Egypt, the men would have to return. On this reading the offer was never a step toward obedience but a way to keep control while appearing to yield.

views.label: A real, if inadequate, concession under pressure
views.case: Others note that this is further than Pharaoh had gone before. He had earlier offered worship inside Egypt, Exodus 8:25, then worship nearby, Exodus 8:28. His own officials were urging release, verse 7, and his offer shows the pressure working. On this view the story traces a king slowly giving ground, one plague at a time.

debates.bearing: Both readings see movement, but the text judges it by God's demand, not by how far Pharaoh had come. Moses and Aaron are driven out, verse 11, because the offer still treated Israel's families as Pharaoh's property. Obedience that keeps back what God has claimed is not yet obedience.

debates.question: Where did the locusts go: the Red Sea or a "Sea of Reeds"?

views.label: The Red Sea, including its northern gulfs
views.case: The Hebrew yam suf is used in 1 Kings 9:26 for the water at Ezion-geber near Eloth, which is the Gulf of Aqaba. It clearly can mean the Red Sea and its arms, and a strong wind from the west would carry a swarm from Egypt toward the Gulf of Suez. The Septuagint also rendered the phrase as the Red Sea, and the New Testament follows it, Hebrews 11:29.

views.label: A reedy body of water near the eastern Delta
views.case: The word suf means reeds, as in the reeds where the infant Moses was placed, Exodus 2:3, and the BSB footnote at verse 19 offers "the Sea of Reeds." Some therefore locate the sea of the locusts and of the later crossing in the lakes and marshes along Egypt's eastern border.

debates.bearing: The location of the crossing is debated, but the literary point is clear either way. The sea that swallows every locust in verse 19 is the same sea that will swallow Pharaoh's army in Exodus 15:4, and the phrase "not a single" returns in Exodus 14:28, "Not one of them survived." The locusts are a preview of the end of Egypt's power.

debates.question: What does God mean by saying He "dealt severely" with the Egyptians, verse 2?

views.label: God made a mockery of Egypt's pride
views.case: The verb is used when Balaam says his donkey has "made a fool of me," Numbers 22:29, and when Saul fears the Philistines will abuse him, 1 Samuel 31:4. On this reading God is saying He toyed with Pharaoh, exposing the king who claimed divine power as helpless before the God of slaves.

views.label: God dealt harshly and decisively
views.case: Others stress the sense of rough or severe dealing, as the BSB has it, and note that the Philistine priests used the same verb when they remembered what God had done to Egypt, 1 Samuel 6:6, translated "afflicted them." The emphasis falls on judgment, not ridicule.

debates.bearing: The two readings overlap. The point is that the proud king becomes a spectacle, and the one who treated Israel as a plaything is shown to be powerless. It is not a portrait of God enjoying cruelty, for the same chapter shows Him removing the locusts the moment Moses prays.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 contains a striking verb, hit'allalti, from the root alal in its reflexive form. It describes dealing with someone roughly, or making sport of them. Balaam uses it when he says to his donkey, "You have made a fool of me!" Numbers 22:29, and the Philistines use it centuries later of what God did to Egypt, 1 Samuel 6:6. The BSB's "how severely I dealt" is a fair rendering, but the word carries an edge of humiliation: Pharaoh, who styled himself a god, was being shown up.

The same verse tells Moses to "tell" his children, and the Hebrew is literally "recount in the ears of your son." The verb sapar in this stem means to recount or rehearse, and it is the verb of Psalm 78:4, where Israel promises to "declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD." It is also related to the ordinary Hebrew words for counting and number. Israel was to go over God's deeds one by one, the way one counts.

In verse 3 Moses asks how long Pharaoh will refuse "to humble yourself," using the root anah, to be low or to be bowed down. In its active stem the same root describes the Egyptians' oppression of Israel: the taskmasters were appointed "to oppress them," and "the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied," Exodus 1:11-12. The oppressor is now asked to take the low place he forced on others. The root returns in Deuteronomy 8:2-3, "He humbled you," where God humbles Israel for their good in the wilderness.

The officials' word "snare," moqesh, verse 7, is the bait or trigger of a hunter's trap. Later the same word warns Israel that Canaan's gods and treaties will become "a snare," Exodus 23:33 and 34:12. Egypt thinks Moses is the trap. The Torah will insist that the real trap is idolatry.

The locust itself is arbeh, a word often connected with the verb rabah, "to be many." When Joel describes his swarm, four locust words appear in turn, gazam, arbeh, yeleq and chasil, which the BSB renders the "devouring," "swarming," "young" and "destroying" locust, Joel 1:4. The two books share the vocabulary as well as the image.

Two phrases describe the swarm's scale. The locusts "cover the face of the land," verse 5, literally "the eye of the land," so thickly that the ground cannot be seen. The same expression is used of Israel itself in Numbers 22:5 and 22:11, where the king of Moab complains that a people come out of Egypt "cover the face of the land." The nation that watched the locusts now looks like a swarm to its enemies. And verse 14 says the swarm was "very heavy," kaved meod, the same phrase used for the hail in Exodus 9:18. The weight Pharaoh put on his heart keeps coming back on his land.

Finally, the winds. The "east wind," ruach qadim, verse 13, is the same wind that will drive back the sea in Exodus 14:21. The wind that removes the locusts is literally a "sea wind," ruach yam, verse 19, which means a west wind for someone living in Canaan with the Mediterranean to the west. Pharaoh's own name for the plague is telling: he asks God to remove "this death," hammavet hazzeh, verse 17. He knows a famine is coming, and he names it truly.

typology.type: The locust army and the Day of the LORD, Joel 1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: Joel takes the eighth plague and turns it toward Israel. The swarm becomes God's "great army," Joel 2:25, the herald of the Day of the LORD, and the only safe response is the one Pharaoh refused, to return with all the heart, Joel 2:12-13. Then the direction changes: the years the locusts ate will be repaid, and God will pour out His Spirit on all people, Joel 2:28. Peter says that promise is what happened at Pentecost, Acts 2:16-21. The escalation is from a ruined harvest restored to a people remade by the Spirit. The type falls short because Egypt's locusts brought no restoration.

typology.type: Telling the children, Exodus 10:2, and the Lord's Supper
typology.fulfillment: God designed Israel's memory so that each generation would recount His deeds to the next, a pattern built into the Passover, Exodus 12:26-27. Jesus gives His church a meal of remembrance on the night of the Passover, "do this in remembrance of Me," Luke 22:19. Paul adds that eating it is itself a proclamation: "you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes," 1 Corinthians 11:26. The escalation is that the church retells not a judgment on Egypt but the death that rescues from judgment. The type falls short because Israel's retelling looked back only, while the Supper also looks forward to His return.

typology.type: The locusts driven into the sea, Exodus 10:19
typology.fulfillment: The wind lifted every locust and dropped it into the sea until not one remained. Micah draws on the exodus when he looks for forgiveness, "As in the days when you came out of Egypt, I will show My wonders," and ends, "You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea," Micah 7:15 and 7:19. In Christ that is what God does with the sins of His people: He removes them completely, having canceled the record against us, Colossians 2:14. The type falls short because the locusts were a plague on Egypt, while Micah's sins are the people's own, and only grace could carry them away.

typology.type: The whole people claimed for worship, Exodus 10:9
typology.fulfillment: Moses insisted that young and old, sons and daughters, all go to hold the feast. Pharaoh tried to keep the children back. The gospel repeats the claim. Jesus says, "Let the little children come to Me, and do not hinder them," Mark 10:14, and Peter tells the crowd at Pentecost that "this promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off," Acts 2:39. The escalation is that the family of the redeemed now reaches beyond Israel's households to all whom the Lord calls. The type falls short because Moses could only demand; Christ draws people to Himself.

study.christ:
The chapter's central demand, "How long will you refuse to humble yourself before Me?" verse 3, finds its answer in Christ by contrast. Pharaoh was a king who would not bow. Jesus is the King who did. Though He was in the form of God, "He humbled Himself and became obedient to death, even death on a cross," Philippians 2:8. The very next words say, "Therefore God exalted Him," Philippians 2:9. Pharaoh clung to his throne and lost it; Christ let go of His glory and was given the name above every name. The God who "opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble," 1 Peter 5:5, is revealed in both stories.

It leads to Christ through remembrance. Verse 2 makes storytelling part of God's purpose, and the Passover in chapter 12 turns that storytelling into a meal with a question from the children at its centre. On the night Jesus kept that meal with His disciples He gave it a new focus: "This is My body, given for you; do this in remembrance of Me," Luke 22:19. The church still tells its children what God did, but the deliverance it rehearses is the death and resurrection of Jesus.

It leads to Christ through the children Pharaoh would not release. Moses insisted, "We will go with our sons and daughters," verse 9. When Joel later picks up the locust plague, God's final word is a promise poured out on the same people: "Your sons and daughters will prophesy," Joel 2:28. Peter announced that promise fulfilled by the risen and ascended Christ, who "has poured out what you now see and hear," Acts 2:33, and he added that "this promise belongs to you and your children," Acts 2:39. The sons and daughters Pharaoh wanted to keep are the very people on whom Christ pours His Spirit.

It leads to Christ as the one who removes what destroys. Pharaoh begged Moses to pray that God would take away "this death," verse 17, and a wind carried it into the sea. Pharaoh wanted only the symptom removed. Christ deals with death itself. Through His death He destroyed "him who holds the power of death," Hebrews 2:14, and He will swallow up death forever, 1 Corinthians 15:54.

The links are real but should not be pressed into allegory. The locusts do not stand for sins, and the east wind is not a code for the Spirit. The chapter points to Christ through the humility it demands, the memory it commands, and the whole people it claims for God.
study.god:
The chapter opens with God explaining His own purposes to His servant: "I have hardened his heart... that I may perform these miraculous signs," verse 1, and "that you may tell your children," verse 2. God does not act blindly or in fits of temper. He has reasons, and He shares some of them. He is the God who wants to be known, not only by Egypt but by Israel's grandchildren, and He shapes history with that audience in mind. "So that all of you may know that I am the LORD" is a statement of His desire for relationship.

He is the God who opposes pride. The whole confrontation turns on the question of humility, verse 3. Hannah sang that "He humbles and He exalts," 1 Samuel 2:7, and Nebuchadnezzar, another proud king, learned that God "is able to humble those who walk in pride," Daniel 4:37. God did not need to destroy Pharaoh in a moment. He let the king's own stubbornness bring the land to ruin, until his own officials told him the truth.

He is Lord of the created order down to its smallest creatures and its winds. The locusts come on an east wind that blows for a day and a night and leave on a west wind until "not a single locust remained," verse 19. That precision matters. The same God who can send more locusts than Egypt had ever seen can remove every last one. Nothing in the natural world is outside His command, "powerful wind fulfilling His word," Psalm 148:8.

He claims His whole people. God's demand was never "let some of My people go." He refuses a worship arrangement in which part of His people stays under another master. His ownership of Israel includes the smallest child and the last animal, because they are His, redeemed for His service.

He is merciful even to those who abuse His mercy. Pharaoh asked forgiveness "once more," verse 17. He had broken his word before and would break it again, and God knew it, verse 1. Yet at Moses' prayer the locusts were removed at once. God's patience with Pharaoh is not approval but kindness, the kind Paul says is meant to lead to repentance, Romans 2:4. That God keeps giving relief to a hardened heart is itself a revelation of His character.

For worship, the chapter calls believers to humility before God and to faithfulness in telling His works. To bow before Him willingly is to learn the lesson Pharaoh refused, and to tell our children what He has done is to take part in the very purpose for which He acted.

crossReferences.note: Joel opens with the same charge as Exodus 10:2, "Tell it to your children," and describes a devastation by four kinds of locust. The prophet deliberately reuses the eighth plague to confront Israel, showing that God's people can come under the same judgment that fell on Egypt.

"I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts." God promises to undo the ruin that a locust judgment brings, which Egypt never experienced. The contrast shows the difference between hardened refusal and repentance: for those who return to Him, judgment gives way to restoration.

Peter quotes Joel's promise of the Spirit poured out on "sons and daughters" and announces its fulfilment at Pentecost. The prophecy that began with locusts ends in the gift of the Spirit, and the families Pharaoh tried to hold back are the very ones God fills.

When a son asks what God's laws mean, the father is to say, "We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt," and to recount "great and devastating signs and wonders." This is Exodus 10:2 put into practice, making the plagues the foundation of Israel's instruction of its children.

Israel promises to declare the LORD's wonders to the next generation, so that "children yet to be born" would set their hope in God. The psalm then retells the plagues, including locusts in verse 46, fulfilling the purpose God gave for them in Exodus 10:2.

Among the covenant curses: "You will sow much seed in the field but harvest little, because the locusts will consume it." The plague God sent on Egypt becomes a warning to Israel. Covenant privilege does not make God's people immune to the judgment they once watched fall on others.

God tells Solomon that if He commands "the locust to devour the land" and His people humble themselves and pray, He will forgive and heal their land. The humility Pharaoh refused in Exodus 10:3 is exactly the response God invites from His own people.

Amos sees God preparing locusts against Israel and pleads, "Lord GOD, please forgive!" and God relents. Like Moses, the prophet intercedes and the swarm is turned aside, showing that the God of the plagues is also a God who hears intercession.

Christ "humbled Himself and became obedient to death," and therefore God exalted Him. Pharaoh's refusal to humble himself, Exodus 10:3, ends in ruin; Christ's willing humility ends in exaltation. The two kings show the two ways God deals with pride and humility.

"As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes." The church's meal is a retelling, like the one commanded in Exodus 10:2, but it proclaims a greater deliverance and looks forward to Christ's return.

Locusts rise from the Abyss but may harm only those "who did not have the seal of God on their foreheads." The eighth plague is recast as a demonic torment, and the distinction God made between Egypt and Israel returns as a distinction between those sealed and those not.

Recalling the days "when you came out of Egypt," Micah praises the God who pardons and says, "You will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea." The sea that swallowed the locusts, Exodus 10:19, becomes a picture of how completely God removes His people's sins.

study.oneStory:
At creation God gave "every green plant for food" to the creatures He had made, Genesis 1:30. The eighth plague runs that gift backward. By the time the swarm has passed, "nothing green was left on any tree or plant in all the land of Egypt," verse 15. The plagues are a kind of undoing of creation over a land whose king has set himself against the Creator, and the locusts leave Egypt looking like the formless ground before God spoke.

The chapter also answers the calling given to Abraham, that he would "command his children and his household after him to keep the way of the LORD," Genesis 18:19. God's people were always meant to be a family that passes on the knowledge of God. Here, at the moment of rescue, God tells Moses that the rescue itself is to become the story told to children and grandchildren. Redemption and teaching belong together.

What follows shows why that memory mattered. Israel would forget. The locusts that fell on Egypt were threatened against Israel in Deuteronomy 28, and the prophets saw them come. But Joel shows the direction of God's purposes. Judgment by locusts gives way to a call to return, to the restoration of the years the locusts ate, and to the promise of the Spirit on sons and daughters, young and old, the very people Moses refused to leave behind.

That promise came true when the risen Christ poured out His Spirit at Pentecost. Through Him the family of God is widened to "all who are far off," Acts 2:39, and the story first told in Israelite homes is now told in every nation. The church's retelling centres on the Lord's Supper, where believers remember His death and look for His return.

The story ends in a new creation where nothing is stripped bare. Revelation's last locusts rise from the Abyss, Revelation 9:3, but they are not the last word. In the city of God stands the tree of life, "bearing twelve kinds of fruit and yielding a fresh crop for each month," and its leaves are "for the healing of the nations," Revelation 22:2. The land Egypt's pride left bare is answered by a world where the green never fails.

quiz.q: According to God's own words in verses 1 to 2, what is one purpose of these repeated signs against Egypt?

options.text: So that Israel would tell their children and grandchildren how severely God dealt with Egypt, so that all would know He is the LORD.
options.note: Verse 2 states this purpose directly, establishing generational testimony as an explicit goal of the plagues.

options.text: So that Egypt would forget the events entirely.
options.note: The opposite is stated; the events are meant to be remembered and retold, not forgotten.

options.text: So that Moses could gain personal fame.
options.note: The stated purpose centers on knowing the LORD and passing that knowledge to future generations, not personal fame for Moses.

options.text: No purpose is given for these signs.
options.note: A specific and explicit purpose is given directly in verses 1 to 2.

quiz.q: What did Pharaoh's own officials say to him before this plague fell?

options.text: They urged him to let the people go, asking if he realized Egypt was already in ruins.
options.note: Verse 7 records this direct plea from Pharaoh's own officials.

options.text: The officials had no opinion on the matter.
options.note: Their direct plea to Pharaoh is explicitly quoted in verse 7.

options.text: They encouraged him to resist Moses further.
options.note: The text records the opposite; his officials urged him to relent, not resist further.

options.text: They demanded that Moses be executed.
options.note: No such demand is recorded; their concern was for Egypt's ruined state, urging release of Israel.

quiz.q: What compromise did Pharaoh offer regarding who could leave to worship?

options.text: He made no offer at all in this passage.
options.note: His specific, limited offer is directly quoted in verses 10 to 11.

options.text: Only the men could go, not the women, children, flocks, or herds.
options.note: Verses 10 to 11 record this limited, rejected offer.

options.text: Only the elderly could go.
options.note: The text specifies men in general, not a restriction to only the elderly.

options.text: Everyone could go, with no restrictions at all.
options.note: Pharaoh specifically restricted the offer to men only, not an unconditional release.

quiz.q: What happened to the locusts after Pharaoh's confession and Moses' prayer?

options.text: A strong west wind carried them all into the Red Sea, leaving not a single locust in Egypt.
options.note: Verse 19 records this complete removal in specific, vivid detail.

options.text: They multiplied further after the prayer.
options.note: The opposite occurred; the prayer led to their complete removal.

options.text: The text does not describe what happened to the locusts.
options.note: Their removal is described in specific and vivid detail in verse 19.

options.text: They remained in Egypt indefinitely.
options.note: The text specifically records their total removal, not a lingering presence.

quiz.q: How does Joel's prophecy connect to the imagery of this plague?

options.text: Joel makes no reference to locusts anywhere in his prophecy.
options.note: Locust imagery is actually central to Joel's prophecy in chapters 1 and 2.

options.text: There is no connection between this plague and Joel's prophecy.
options.note: Joel's prophecy draws directly and extensively on locust plague imagery.

options.text: Joel uses locust imagery only to describe blessing, never judgment.
options.note: Joel's initial locust imagery describes judgment; the restoration promise comes afterward as a separate, hopeful message.

options.text: Joel uses locust devastation as an image of judgment, later promising restoration of what the locusts destroyed.
options.note: Joel 1:4 and 2:25 both draw on locust imagery for judgment and eventual restoration.

questions: God's stated purpose was that Israel would tell their children and grandchildren what He had done. What stories of God's faithfulness in your own life are you intentionally passing on to the next generation?

Pharaoh's own officials recognized Egypt was in ruins and urged him to relent, yet he still tried to negotiate limited terms. Where might you be resisting full surrender to God even while everyone around you can see the cost of your resistance?
Pharaoh offered a partial release, men only, holding back what mattered most. What are you still holding back from full obedience to God, hoping a partial commitment will be enough?

Pharaoh's confession, 'I have sinned,' sounded sincere but proved short lived once again. How do you guard your own repentance from becoming merely a reaction to consequences rather than a lasting change of heart?

Joel later transforms locust imagery from judgment into a promise that God will restore the years the locusts have eaten. What area of loss in your own life do you need to trust God can still restore?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew here uses kabed, made heavy, translated hardened, describing both Pharaoh's heart and, notably, the hearts of his officials as well, broadening the hardening beyond Pharaoh alone.
The Hebrew for Red Sea here is more literally the Sea of Reeds, yam suph, the same body of water Israel will later cross in the great deliverance of chapter 14.
